name: John Wycliffe
role: Oxford theologian and philosopher, rector of Lutterworth, reformer

died.date: 31 December 1384, after a stroke suffered while hearing Mass

summary: Oxford theologian who argued that Scripture is the supreme authority for Christians, attacked the wealth and power of the clergy and papacy, and inspired the first complete English Bible and the Lollard movement.

key_dates.label: Becomes rector of Lutterworth; royal envoy to papal negotiators at Bruges
Summoned before the bishops at St Paul's; Pope Gregory XI condemns his teachings
Writes On the Truth of Holy Scripture; the Great Schism divides the papacy
Oxford condemns his teaching on the Eucharist; he withdraws to Lutterworth
Blackfriars Council condemns 24 of his propositions
First complete English Bible produced by his circle (c. 1382; revised c. 1388–1395)

accomplishments.text: Was the leading Oxford philosopher and theologian of his generation: Master of Balliol College and a doctor of theology from 1372.
Argued in On the Truth of Holy Scripture (1378) that the Bible is the highest authority for Christian belief, above church tradition and papal decrees.

Argued in On Civil Dominion (c. 1375–1376) that clergy who lived in sin forfeited their right to property, and that secular rulers could take church wealth. This won him the support of John of Gaunt and other nobles.
Challenged papal power. After the Great Schism of 1378 he argued that a pope who did not follow Christ was not his true representative and could be Antichrist.
Rejected the doctrine of transubstantiation in On the Eucharist (c. 1380). This lost him many supporters and led to his condemnation at Oxford.
Inspired the first complete translation of the Bible into English, made from the Latin Vulgate by his associates (c. 1382, revised c. 1388–1395). How much he translated himself is debated.
His ideas were spread by itinerant preachers and gave rise to the Lollard movement in England.
Influenced Jan Hus and the Bohemian reform. Czech students carried his writings from Oxford to Prague after Richard II married Anne of Bohemia in 1382.
Later Protestant writers called him the "Morning Star of the Reformation."

persecution_note: Wycliffe was condemned by a pope, tried before English bishops, and had his teachings condemned at Oxford and at the Blackfriars Council. Powerful protectors kept him from being imprisoned, and he died a natural death at Lutterworth. His followers, the Lollards, were later persecuted and burned under English law. In 1415 the Council of Constance declared him a heretic, and in 1428 his remains were dug up and burned.

persecution.title: Summoned before the bishops at St Paul's, London
persecution.summary: Wycliffe was called to answer for his preaching before the bishops at St Paul's Cathedral. He came with powerful protectors, and the hearing broke up in a quarrel between the Bishop of London and John of Gaunt before any judgment was given.

responsible.name: William Courtenay
responsible.role: Bishop of London; led the hearing
responsible.jurisdiction: Diocese of London, English Church (under papal authority)

defended_by.name: John of Gaunt
defended_by.role: Duke of Lancaster, the king's son and the most powerful noble in England

persecution.outcome: The hearing ended in disorder, without a verdict.

persecution.title: Condemned by Pope Gregory XI
persecution.summary: Pope Gregory XI issued five bulls condemning 18 propositions from Wycliffe's writings, mostly on church property and authority. He ordered the Archbishop of Canterbury and the Bishop of London to investigate and, if the charges were proved, to imprison him. Separate bulls went to King Edward III and to the University of Oxford.

responsible.name: Simon Sudbury
responsible.role: Archbishop of Canterbury; instructed to act on the bulls

responsible.name: William Courtenay
responsible.role: Bishop of London; instructed to act on the bulls

persecution.outcome: Oxford was reluctant to act against him, and he was not imprisoned.

persecution.title: Hearing at Lambeth Palace
persecution.summary: Acting on the papal bulls, the bishops examined Wycliffe at Lambeth Palace. Before they could pass sentence, a messenger from Joan of Kent, the young King Richard II's mother, forbade them to condemn him, and a London crowd broke into the hearing.

defended_by.name: Joan of Kent
defended_by.role: Princess of Wales, mother of Richard II; forbade the bishops to pass sentence

persecution.outcome: No sentence was passed. He was told to stop teaching the disputed propositions.

persecution.title: Teaching on the Eucharist condemned at Oxford
persecution.summary: The Chancellor of Oxford and a council of doctors condemned Wycliffe's denial of transubstantiation and forbade anyone at the university to teach it, on pain of imprisonment and excommunication.

responsible.name: William Barton
responsible.role: Chancellor of the University of Oxford

persecution.outcome: Wycliffe left Oxford and spent his remaining years at Lutterworth.

persecution.title: The Blackfriars Council and the purge of his Oxford followers
persecution.summary: Archbishop Courtenay held a council at the Blackfriars in London, remembered as the "Earthquake Synod" because an earthquake struck while it met. It condemned 24 propositions drawn from Wycliffe's teaching, 10 as heretical and 14 as erroneous. With royal backing, the archbishop then purged Wycliffe's supporters at Oxford. Nicholas Hereford, Philip Repingdon, and John Aston were suspended and either recanted or fled. Wycliffe himself was not named or summoned.

responsible.name: William Courtenay
responsible.role: Archbishop of Canterbury (from 1381); convened the council

responsible.name: Blackfriars Council
responsible.role: Bishops and theologians who condemned the propositions

responsible.name: Richard II
responsible.role: King of England; authorized the arrest of unlicensed preachers

persecution.outcome: Wycliffite teaching was driven out of Oxford. Wycliffe kept writing at Lutterworth until his death.

persecution.title: Lollards burned under English law; English Bible restricted
persecution.summary: Wycliffe's followers, the Lollards, were hunted after his death. In 1401 Parliament passed the statute De heretico comburendo, which allowed convicted heretics to be burned, and William Sawtrey became the first Lollard executed. Archbishop Arundel's Constitutions of Oxford (1407–1409) banned new English translations of the Bible, and the reading of unapproved ones, without a bishop's permission. Sir John Oldcastle, a Lollard leader, was executed in 1417.

responsible.name: Henry IV
responsible.role: King of England; approved the 1401 statute

responsible.name: Thomas Arundel
responsible.role: Archbishop of Canterbury; issued the Constitutions of Oxford

persecution.outcome: Lollardy went underground but survived until the English Reformation.

persecution.title: Declared a heretic at Constance; remains dug up and burned
persecution.summary: On 4 May 1415 the Council of Constance condemned Wycliffe as a heretic, condemned articles drawn from his writings, ordered his books burned, and ordered his remains removed from consecrated ground. The order was carried out in 1428 at the command of Pope Martin V. Richard Fleming, Bishop of Lincoln, had his bones dug up at Lutterworth and burned, and the ashes were thrown into the River Swift.

responsible.name: Council of Constance
responsible.jurisdiction: General council of the Western Church

responsible.name: Pope Martin V
responsible.role: Ordered the exhumation to be carried out

responsible.name: Richard Fleming
responsible.role: Bishop of Lincoln; carried out the exhumation

persecution.outcome: His remains were burned and scattered in the River Swift in 1428.

Stephen E. Lahey, John Wyclif, Great Medieval Thinkers (New York: Oxford University Press, 2009).
